At the project's construction and spoil areas outside the impoundment site, a temporary loss of existing limited recreation opportunities would occur. Applicant intends to slope and seed these areas after construction, thereby ultimately restoring them for limited recreational opportunities similar to those now available.
5.3 LOSS OF ENVIRONMENTAL QUALITY
5.3.1 Aquatic Fauna
During the construction period, and for an unknown duration required for stream recovery, the stream habitats and aquatic community of Howard Creek would be adversely impacted by silt-laden runoff from the proposed Bad Creek Project. Populations of benthic organisms would likely be reduced by increased siltation in Howard Creek. Populations of larval amphibians would be reduced or possibly eliminated in those reaches of Howard Creek receiving heavy siltation (Dysart, et al., 1973). Trout populations would suffer losses due to reduction of their benthic food sources and the effects of increased sedimentation on spawning gravels. It is possible that reduced flows, in conjunction with higher sediment loads, would further reduce the suitability of Howard Creek for trout production below its confluence with Bad Creek and West Bad Creek for an indeterminate period, depending on the time required for the stream to recover from siltation caused by construction and clearing activities.
A localized increase in turbidity would be expected in the northwest arm of Lake Jocissee at its confluence with Howard Creek and near the inlet-outlet structure. Such an increase would have a short-term effect, lasting until after disturbed areas in the Bad Creek, West Bad Creek, and Howard Creek basins had been regrassed or reforested and stabilization of the upper reservoir had occurred. During the period of increased turbidities, local fish populations might migrate to adjacent areas of Lake Jocassee.
Clearing of the proposed construction yard area could create localized siltation and turbid water conditions in the Whitewater River near its confluence with Lake Jocassee and the upper Whitewater arm of Lake Jocassee during periods of heavy rainfall and runoff. The aquatic ecosystem could be adversely affected during such periods, but the effects would be short-term, terminating when vegetative cover was reestablished in the construction yard area.
